subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Harvest: Finding Area, Volume, and Balance
hook: A farmer's daughter learns calculus by measuring fields and grain stores

slides.title: Application of Integrals
slides.storyContext: Priya returns to her village for summer break and discovers that calculus isn't abstract—it's alive in the fields, granaries, and river embankments all around her.

slides.title: The Village Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya's father Babuji wants to know the exact area of an irregularly shaped wheat field bounded by the river's curve y = 6x - x² and the irrigation channel y = 0. The government surveyor Ravi says he'll charge 5,000 rupees. Priya says, 'Babuji, I can find it using integrals!' Her father laughs—but she's serious. When she gets the answer in minutes, Babuji realizes his daughter has learned something powerful.

slides.title: Area Between Two Curves
slides.storyContext: Priya draws the boundary curves in the dust. The field is trapped between the parabola y = 6x - x² (the river's curve, opening downward) and the x-axis (the irrigation channel). To find area, she integrates.

points.label: Definition
points.text: The area A between curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) from x = a to x = b (where f(x) ≥ g(x)) is: A = ∫[a to b] (f(x) - g(x)) dx

points.label: Finding limits
points.text: First find where the curves intersect by solving f(x) = g(x). These are the bounds of integration.

points.label: Orientation
points.text: Always integrate (upper curve) − (lower curve). If uncertain, sketch or evaluate at a test point.

example.problem: Priya's field: find area between y = 6x - x² and y = 0. Step 1: Find intersections. 6x - x² = 0 → x(6 - x) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 6. Step 2: Set up integral. A = ∫[0 to 6] (6x - x² - 0) dx = ∫[0 to 6] (6x - x²) dx. Step 3: Integrate. ∫(6x - x²) dx = 3x² - x³/3 + C. Step 4: Evaluate. A = [3(6)² - (6)³/3] − [0] = [108 - 72] = 36 square units.
example.solution: Area = 36 square units. When surveyor Ravi measures it later, he gets the same answer. Priya's father is amazed—no fee charged!

slides.inSimpleWords: To find the area of a region trapped between two curves, subtract the lower curve from the upper curve, then integrate.

slides.title: Volume of Solids of Revolution
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother asks her to estimate how much grain can fit in the large earthen pot in the store. The pot is shaped like a solid of revolution—the potter rotated a curve around a vertical axis to form it. Priya realizes: this is calculus!

points.label: Disk Method
points.text: When curve y = f(x) is rotated about the x-axis, volume V = π ∫[a to b] [f(x)]² dx. Each thin slice is a disk with radius f(x).

points.label: Washer Method
points.text: When region between two curves is rotated, V = π ∫[a to b] ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx, where R = outer radius, r = inner radius.

points.label: Shell Method
points.text: Alternatively, rotate about y-axis using shells: V = 2π ∫[a to b] x · f(x) dx.

example.problem: The potter shapes a pot by rotating y = √x (from x = 0 to x = 4) about the x-axis. Find volume. Using disk method: V = π ∫[0 to 4] (√x)² dx = π ∫[0 to 4] x dx = π [x²/2][0 to 4] = π (8 − 0) = 8π cubic units.
example.solution: Volume = 8π ≈ 25.13 cubic units. Priya tells her mother, 'This pot holds about 25 liters of grain!'

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotate a curve around an axis and use integrals to find the volume of the solid created.

slides.title: Arc Length
slides.storyContext: Ravi the surveyor needs to measure the length of the river's curve that borders Priya's field—for a water-maintenance project. He can't just pace it out. Priya says, 'Use arc length integration!'

points.label: Arc Length Formula
points.text: For smooth curve y = f(x) from x = a to x = b, arc length L = ∫[a to b] √(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx

points.label: Parametric form
points.text: If curve is x = x(t), y = y(t), then L = ∫[α to β] √([dx/dt]² + [dy/dt]²) dt

example.problem: Find arc length of y = 6x - x² from x = 0 to x = 6 (Priya's field boundary). Step 1: Compute derivative. dy/dx = 6 - 2x. Step 2: Set up integral. L = ∫[0 to 6] √(1 + (6 - 2x)²) dx = ∫[0 to 6] √(1 + 36 - 24x + 4x²) dx = ∫[0 to 6] √(4x² - 24x + 37) dx. Step 3: This integral is complex (complete the square, use substitution). After integration, L ≈ 10.7 units.
example.solution: The river's curve is approximately 10.7 units long. Ravi uses this to plan maintenance work.

slides.inSimpleWords: To measure the true length of a curved path, integrate the rate of change in both x and y directions.

slides.title: Surface Area of Revolution
slides.storyContext: A metalsmith in the village wants to make decorative water vessels by rotating metal bands into smooth surfaces. Priya helps calculate how much metal is needed—by finding surface area.

points.label: Surface Area Formula (about x-axis)
points.text: S = 2π ∫[a to b] f(x) · √(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx

points.label: Surface Area Formula (about y-axis)
points.text: S = 2π ∫[a to b] x · √(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx

example.problem: Rotate y = √x (x ∈ [0, 4]) about x-axis. Surface area: S = 2π ∫[0 to 4] √x · √(1 + 1/(4x)) dx = 2π ∫[0 to 4] √x · √((4x + 1)/(4x)) dx. After simplification and integration, S ≈ 30.8 square units.
example.solution: The metalsmith needs enough material to cover approximately 30.8 square units of surface.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you rotate a curve around an axis, the surface it sweeps has area = circumference at each point × arc length element.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Grain Silo
slides.storyContext: Babuji plans to build a silo for storing grain. It's shaped like a cone with height 8 m and base radius 3 m, formed by rotating the line y = (3/8)x about the y-axis for 0 ≤ y ≤ 8. Find total volume.

example.problem: A cone is formed by rotating y-values from 0 to 8; at height y, the radius is (3/8) × 8 = 3 at the base, scaling linearly. Using disk method (integrating perpendicular to axis of rotation): at height y, radius r(y) = (3y)/8. Volume = π ∫[0 to 8] [(3y)/8]² dy = π ∫[0 to 8] (9y²/64) dy = (9π/64) × [y³/3][0 to 8] = (9π/64) × (512/3) = (9π × 512)/(64 × 3) = 24π cubic meters.
example.solution: Volume = 24π ≈ 75.4 cubic meters. Babuji can store roughly 75 cubic meters of grain—enough for the monsoon!

slides.inSimpleWords: Real silo volumes are found using calculus, not guesswork.

slides.title: Test Yourself: The River Bridge
slides.storyContext: A new bridge arches over the river, shaped like y = 4 - x² (for -2 ≤ x ≤ 2, measured in meters from the center). Find (a) the area under the arch (cross-sectional area if water fills under it), and (b) the arc length of the arch itself.

points.text: (a) Integrate to find area between y = 4 - x² and y = 0.
(b) Use dy/dx = -2x to set up and evaluate arc length integral.

example.problem: (a) Area = ∫[-2 to 2] (4 - x²) dx = [4x - x³/3][-2 to 2] = (8 - 8/3) − (−8 + 8/3) = (16/3) − (−16/3) = 32/3 ≈ 10.67 m². (b) Arc length = ∫[-2 to 2] √(1 + 4x²) dx ≈ 9.29 m (use numerical methods or table of integrals).
example.solution: Area ≈ 10.67 m²; Arc length ≈ 9.29 m. Engineers use these to plan reinforcement.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply area and arc length formulas to a real-world bridge design.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Area between curves: integrate (upper − lower) over the region.
Volume by revolution: use disk, washer, or shell methods depending on axis and region.
Arc length: ∫√(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx measures true path length.
Surface area of revolution: 2π × radius × arc element.
Always sketch the region, identify bounds, and choose the right method.
Real applications: crop fields, storage vessels, bridge designs, water infrastructure.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integrals measure areas, volumes, lengths, and surface areas of real-world shapes.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Medicine: How Things Change Over Time
hook: A pharmacist's son learns how differential equations predict medicine levels in the blood

slides.title: Differential Equations
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices that when his father dispenses medicine, doctors always ask: 'How fast does it leave the body?' This rate of change is governed by differential equations—the heartbeat of physics, biology, and engineering.

slides.title: The Medication Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun's younger sister takes an antibiotic. The dosage is 250 mg at noon. By evening, the nurse measures the drug concentration in her blood: 200 mg. By next morning: 160 mg. Arjun asks his father, 'Is she getting worse?' Dr. Meena smiles. 'No—the body eliminates a fixed fraction of drug every few hours. If we know this rate, we can predict concentration at any time.' Arjun thinks: 'That sounds like a differential equation!' He's right.

slides.title: What is a Differential Equation?
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi, Arjun's teacher, draws an equation on the board involving a function y and its derivative dy/dx. 'This is a differential equation—it says how y changes as x changes.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A differential equation is an equation relating a function y and its derivatives dy/dx, d²y/dx², etc.

points.label: Order
points.text: The order is the highest derivative present. dy/dx + 2y = 0 is first-order. d²y/dx² - 5dy/dx + 6y = 0 is second-order.

points.label: Solution
points.text: A solution is a function y(x) that satisfies the equation when substituted back.

points.label: General vs Particular
points.text: General solution has arbitrary constants (C₁, C₂, ...). Particular solution results from initial conditions (y at a specific x).

example.problem: Consider dy/dx = 3x². Find the general solution. Integrate: y = ∫3x² dx = x³ + C. Verify: dy/dx = d(x³ + C)/dx = 3x². ✓
example.solution: General solution is y = x³ + C. If y(0) = 5 (initial condition), then 5 = 0 + C, so C = 5 and particular solution is y = x³ + 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: A differential equation relates a quantity and how fast it changes. The solution is the quantity as a function.

slides.title: Separable Differential Equations
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi teaches: 'Some equations are easy to solve if we can separate variables.' Arjun sees this as the key to the medicine problem.

points.label: Form
points.text: An equation of the form dy/dx = f(x) · g(y) is separable if we can rearrange as dy/g(y) = f(x) dx.

points.label: Method
points.text: Integrate both sides: ∫(1/g(y)) dy = ∫f(x) dx + C.

points.label: Exponential decay
points.text: Common in nature: dM/dt = -kM (medicine leaving body). Solution: M(t) = M₀ e^(-kt), where M₀ is initial amount.

example.problem: Model Arjun's sister's medicine: dM/dt = -0.1M, where M is drug amount in mg and t is time in hours. Initial dose M(0) = 250 mg. Separate: dM/M = -0.1 dt. Integrate: ln|M| = -0.1t + C. At t=0: ln(250) = C. So ln(M) = -0.1t + ln(250). Solve: M(t) = 250 e^(-0.1t). At t=8 (evening): M(8) = 250 e^(-0.8) ≈ 250 × 0.449 ≈ 112 mg. At t=24 (next morning): M(24) = 250 e^(-2.4) ≈ 250 × 0.091 ≈ 23 mg.
example.solution: M(t) = 250 e^(-0.1t). The concentration decays exponentially. After 24 hours, only ~23 mg remains, so a second dose is needed.

slides.inSimpleWords: If a rate of change is proportional to the quantity (dy/dx = ky), the solution is exponential growth or decay.

slides.title: Linear Differential Equations of Order 1
slides.storyContext: Not all real-world problems decay purely exponentially. Sometimes there's an external input—like Arjun's sister getting a new dose of medicine while the old one is still leaving her body.

points.label: Standard form
points.text: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x), where P and Q are functions of x.

points.label: Integrating factor
points.text: Multiply both sides by e^(∫P(x) dx). Left side becomes d/dx[e^(∫P dx) · y].

points.label: Solution
points.text: y = e^(-∫P dx) · ∫Q · e^(∫P dx) dx + C · e^(-∫P dx)

example.problem: Suppose sister takes 250 mg at noon, then 100 mg more at 6 PM, and body eliminates 10% per hour. Model as dy/dx + 0.1y = (input), where input is 0 until 6 PM, then becomes a new dose. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 6: dy/dt + 0.1y = 0. Solution: y = 250 e^(-0.1t). At t = 6, y(6) = 250 e^(-0.6) ≈ 136 mg. Then at t = 6, add 100 mg: new initial condition y(6) = 236 mg. For t > 6: solve anew with y(6) = 236.
example.solution: y(t) = 250 e^(-0.1t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6, then y(t) ≈ 236 e^(-0.1(t-6)) for t > 6. Concentrations accumulate until body's elimination exceeds intake.

slides.inSimpleWords: If a quantity both decays and receives new input, use linear DE methods to track the balance.

slides.title: Applications in Science and Engineering
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi shows Arjun real examples: Newton's law of cooling, bacterial growth, radioactive decay, electrical circuits, population dynamics. All are differential equations.

points.label: Newton's Law of Cooling
points.text: dT/dt = -k(T - Tₐ), where T is object temp, Tₐ is ambient temp. Solution: T(t) = Tₐ + (T₀ - Tₐ)e^(-kt).

points.label: Logistic Growth (population)
points.text: dP/dt = rP(1 - P/K), where r is growth rate, K is carrying capacity. Realistic because growth slows as population approaches limit.

points.label: RL circuits (electricity)
points.text: L(dI/dt) + RI = V, where L is inductance, R is resistance, V is voltage. Current I reaches steady state V/R.

example.problem: Hot tea at 80°C placed in room at 25°C. Cooling constant k = 0.05 min⁻¹. What's temperature after 10 minutes? T(10) = 25 + (80 - 25)e^(-0.05×10) = 25 + 55e^(-0.5) ≈ 25 + 55 × 0.606 ≈ 25 + 33.3 ≈ 58.3°C.
example.solution: After 10 minutes, tea is about 58°C—still too hot to drink, but cooling steadily toward room temperature.

slides.inSimpleWords: Differential equations model how real quantities change: temperature, population, current, concentration.

slides.title: Homogeneous and Non-homogeneous Equations
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi distinguishes two types of linear equations: those with only y (homogeneous) and those with an extra term (non-homogeneous, like our medicine dose model).

points.label: Homogeneous
points.text: dy/dx + P(x)y = 0. Solution always has the form y = Ce^(-∫P dx).

points.label: Non-homogeneous
points.text: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x), where Q(x) ≠ 0. General solution = (homogeneous solution) + (particular solution).

points.label: Finding particular solution
points.text: Use variation of parameters or method of undetermined coefficients depending on form of Q.

example.problem: Solve dy/dx - 2y = e^(3x). Step 1: Homogeneous part. dy/dx - 2y = 0 has solution yₕ = Ce^(2x). Step 2: Particular solution. Try yₚ = Ae^(3x). Then dyₚ/dx = 3Ae^(3x). Substitute: 3Ae^(3x) - 2Ae^(3x) = e^(3x), so Ae^(3x) = e^(3x), thus A = 1. Step 3: General solution: y = Ce^(2x) + e^(3x).
example.solution: y = Ce^(2x) + e^(3x). With initial condition y(0) = 0: 0 = C + 1, so C = -1, giving y = e^(3x) - e^(2x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Equations with external inputs (like medicine doses) are non-homogeneous. Solve by combining two parts: natural decay and forced response.

slides.title: Full Problem: Antibiotic Therapy
slides.storyContext: Arjun calculates a complete antibiotic model. Dose is 200 mg every 12 hours. Body eliminates 15% per hour. What's the concentration just before the 4th dose (after 36 hours)?

example.problem: Between doses, dM/dt = -0.15M. At each dose, M increases by 200 mg. Solve piecewise: After 1st dose (t=0): M₀ = 200. At t=12⁻ (just before 2nd dose): M = 200e^(-0.15×12) = 200e^(-1.8) ≈ 200 × 0.165 ≈ 33 mg. After 2nd dose: M = 33 + 200 = 233. At t=24⁻: M = 233e^(-1.8) ≈ 38.5 mg. After 3rd dose: M = 38.5 + 200 = 238.5. At t=36⁻ (before 4th dose): M = 238.5e^(-1.8) ≈ 39.4 mg.
example.solution: Just before the 4th dose, concentration is about 39.4 mg. After the 4th dose, it's 239.4 mg. The concentration stabilizes near this level after a few doses.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real therapies involve repeated dosing and exponential elimination—use DEs to predict safe levels.

slides.title: Test Yourself: Water Tank Drainage
slides.storyContext: A cylindrical tank holds water. A tap at the bottom drains it. The rate of drainage is proportional to the square root of the height of water: dh/dt = -k√h, where k = 0.1, h is height in meters.

points.text: If h(0) = 1 meter, find h(t).
How long until the tank is empty (h = 0)?

example.problem: Separate: dh/√h = -0.1 dt. Integrate: 2√h = -0.1t + C. At t = 0, h = 1: 2√1 = C, so C = 2. Thus 2√h = -0.1t + 2, so √h = 1 - 0.05t, hence h = (1 - 0.05t)². Tank empty when 1 - 0.05t = 0, i.e., t = 20 seconds.
example.solution: h(t) = (1 - 0.05t)² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 20. Tank empties in 20 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Separable equations model realistic draining and filling processes in engineering.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A differential equation relates a function and its rate of change.
Order is the highest derivative; solution satisfies the equation.
Separable DEs: rearrange to get all y terms on one side, x on the other, then integrate.
Exponential decay/growth: M(t) = M₀ e^(kt) is the solution to dM/dt = kM.
Linear first-order DEs use integrating factor method.
Real applications: medicine concentration, cooling, population, circuits, draining tanks.
General solution has arbitrary constants; initial conditions give particular solutions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Differential equations predict how real systems change over time—essential for medicine, physics, engineering, biology.

subject: Mathematics
title: Kavya's Dance: Motion, Force, and Direction
hook: A dancer discovers how vectors describe both position and movement on stage

slides.title: Vector Algebra
slides.storyContext: Kavya practices Bharatanatyam in her studio. Every move has direction and magnitude—steps, turns, hand movements. Her choreographer Ramesh says, 'This is vector algebra,' and Kavya's eyes light up.

slides.title: The Choreography Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ramesh is choreographing a group dance. He needs to describe where each dancer should move. He tells Kavya, 'Start at center. Move 3 meters east, then 4 meters north. Where do you end up?' Kavya thinks: 'That's not just about distance—it's about direction too!' Ramesh's brother Pradeep, a physics teacher, hears this and says, 'That's vector addition!' He shows them how vectors make dance positioning precise.

slides.title: Scalars and Vectors
slides.storyContext: Pradeep draws on a board: 'A scalar is just a number—like distance traveled (5 km). A vector has both magnitude and direction—like displacement (5 km north).'

points.label: Scalar
points.text: Quantity with magnitude only. Examples: distance (5 m), mass (70 kg), temperature (37°C).

points.label: Vector
points.text: Quantity with magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement (5 m north), velocity (20 m/s east), force (10 N downward).

points.label: Notation
points.text: Vectors are written as →AB or boldface v, or with arrow: $\vec{v}$. Magnitude is |→v| or just v.

points.label: Components
points.text: In 2D, vector v is written as v = (vₓ, vᵧ) or v = vₓ î + vᵧ ĵ, where î, ĵ are unit vectors along x, y axes.

example.problem: Kavya's first move: 3 meters east, 4 meters north. Using axes (east=x, north=y), displacement vector d = (3, 4) or d = 3î + 4ĵ. Magnitude |d| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 meters. Direction: angle θ = arctan(4/3) ≈ 53.1° from east.
example.solution: Her displacement is a vector of magnitude 5 m at 53.1° north of east. She ends up 5 meters away from center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scalars are just numbers; vectors have size and direction. Use components to calculate exact positions.

slides.title: Vector Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Kavya makes a second move: 2 meters west, 1 meter south. Ramesh asks, 'What's your total displacement?' This requires adding vectors.

points.label: Component addition
points.text: If u = (uₓ, uᵧ) and v = (vₓ, vᵧ), then u + v = (uₓ + vₓ, uᵧ + vᵧ).

points.label: Graphical method
points.text: Place tail of second vector at head of first; resultant goes from tail of first to head of second (triangle/parallelogram rule).

points.label: Subtraction
points.text: u - v = u + (-v). Vector -v has same magnitude but opposite direction.

example.problem: Kavya's first move: d₁ = (3, 4). Second move: 2 meters west (−2 m, 0), 1 meter south (0, −1), so d₂ = (−2, −1). Total displacement: d = d₁ + d₂ = (3, 4) + (−2, −1) = (1, 3). Magnitude: |d| = √(1² + 3²) = √10 ≈ 3.16 meters. Direction: θ = arctan(3/1) ≈ 71.6° from east.
example.solution: After both moves, Kavya is 3.16 meters away from center, at about 71.6° north of east.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add vectors by adding their components separately. Subtract by adding the negative vector.

slides.title: Dot Product (Scalar Product)
slides.storyContext: Pradeep introduces the dot product: 'This tells us how much two vectors align or point in the same direction.' Ramesh uses this to calculate work in a dance lift.

points.label: Definition
points.text: For vectors u = (uₓ, uᵧ, u_z) and v = (vₓ, vᵧ, v_z), dot product u·v = uₓvₓ + uᵧvᵧ + u_zv_z.

points.label: Geometric form
points.text: u·v = |u| |v| cos(θ), where θ is angle between vectors.

points.label: Properties
points.text: u·v = v·u (commutative). If θ = 90°, then u·v = 0 (perpendicular vectors have zero dot product).

points.label: Work in physics
points.text: Work W = F·d = |F| |d| cos(θ), where F is force, d is displacement.

example.problem: In a dance lift, Pradeep models a dancer (Kavya) and partner (another performer). Force applied by partner: F = (40, 30, 10) N (x, y, z components). Displacement of Kavya: d = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) m. Work = F·d = 40(0.5) + 30(0.3) + 10(0.2) = 20 + 9 + 2 = 31 joules.
example.solution: Work done in the lift is 31 joules. Since this is positive, the lift raises Kavya successfully.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dot product measures how two vectors align. Multiply corresponding components and add them up.

slides.title: Cross Product (Vector Product)
slides.storyContext: Pradeep says, 'The cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both original vectors. In dance, this describes rotation or torque.' Ramesh uses it for spinning moves.

points.label: Definition (3D)
points.text: u × v = (uᵧv_z − u_zv_y, u_zv_x − uₓv_z, uₓv_y − uᵧv_x). Written as determinant: u × v = | î  ĵ  k̂ | | uₓ uᵧ u_z | | vₓ vᵧ v_z |

points.label: Magnitude
points.text: |u × v| = |u| |v| sin(θ), where θ is angle between u and v.

points.label: Direction
points.text: u × v is perpendicular to both u and v. Direction given by right-hand rule: curl fingers from u to v; thumb points in direction of u × v.

points.label: Torque
points.text: Torque τ = r × F, where r is position vector, F is force. Magnitude tells how strongly rotation occurs.

example.problem: Kavya spins around a vertical axis. Her position from axis: r = (2, 0, 0) meters. Force applied (by her muscles): F = (0, 10, 5) N. Torque: τ = r × F. Using determinant formula: τ = | î  ĵ  k̂ | | 2  0  0 | | 0 10 5 | = î(0×5 − 0×10) − ĵ(2×5 − 0×0) + k̂(2×10 − 0×0) = 0î − 10ĵ + 20k̂ = (0, −10, 20). Magnitude: |τ| = √(0² + 10² + 20²) = √500 ≈ 22.4 N·m.
example.solution: Torque is about 22.4 N·m pointing mostly upward (positive z), causing clockwise spin when viewed from above.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cross product gives a perpendicular vector. Its magnitude shows how strongly two vectors 'rotate' around each other.

slides.title: Unit Vectors and Direction Cosines
slides.storyContext: Pradeep teaches Kavya how to describe exact directions. 'A unit vector points in a direction with length 1. Use it as a compass.'

points.label: Unit vector
points.text: u-hat = u / |u| gives unit vector in direction of u.

points.label: Direction cosines
points.text: For vector v making angles α, β, γ with x, y, z axes: cos(α), cos(β), cos(γ) are direction cosines. cos²(α) + cos²(β) + cos²(γ) = 1.

points.label: Standard basis
points.text: î = (1, 0, 0), ĵ = (0, 1, 0), k̂ = (0, 0, 1) are unit vectors along coordinate axes.

example.problem: Kavya's displacement d = (3, 4) meters. Find unit vector in this direction. |d| = 5. Unit vector: d-hat = (3/5, 4/5) = (0.6, 0.8). Direction cosines (2D): cos(α) = 0.6 (angle from x-axis ≈ 53.1°), cos(β) = 0.8 (angle from y-axis ≈ 36.9°). Verify: 0.6² + 0.8² = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1. ✓
example.solution: Unit vector is (0.6, 0.8). This tells exactly which way Kavya is facing after her first displacement.

slides.inSimpleWords: Unit vectors and direction cosines give precise compass directions for any displacement.

slides.title: Full Problem: Group Dance Positioning
slides.storyContext: Ramesh choreographs a formation of four dancers. Kavya at A starts at center (0, 0). Three others start at B = (3, 4), C = (−2, 5), D = (4, −1) in meters. What's the center of mass of the group?

example.problem: Center of mass = (sum of position vectors) / (number of dancers) = (A + B + C + D) / 4 = [(0, 0) + (3, 4) + (−2, 5) + (4, −1)] / 4 = (5, 8) / 4 = (1.25, 2). Kavya confirms: the choreography centers around (1.25, 2), about 2.4 meters from stage center.
example.solution: Center of mass is at (1.25, 2). Ramesh uses this to plan the group's pivot point for synchronized turns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vector algebra helps choreograph group formations by calculating positions and centers.

slides.title: Test Yourself: Lift and Rotation
slides.storyContext: Two dancers: A at (0, 0) and B at (2, 3). They dance a move where A lifts B upward (in the z direction) by 1 meter, then they both rotate together. Use vectors to find B's new position.

points.text: Initial position of B: (2, 3, 0).
After lift: B moves to (2, 3, 1).
Find displacement, magnitude, and direction.

example.problem: Initial: B₀ = (2, 3, 0). Final: B₁ = (2, 3, 1). Displacement: Δr = B₁ − B₀ = (0, 0, 1). Magnitude: |Δr| = 1 meter (pure vertical lift). Direction: straight up (along k̂).
example.solution: The lift moves B vertically 1 meter. B ends at (2, 3, 1), now 1 meter higher while maintaining horizontal position.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use vector subtraction to track movement in 3D space during complex choreography.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Scalars are numbers; vectors have magnitude and direction.
Components: v = (vₓ, vᵧ, v_z) or v = vₓ î + vᵧ ĵ + v_z k̂.
Vector addition: add components separately.
Dot product u·v = |u| |v| cos(θ). Zero if perpendicular.
Cross product u × v is perpendicular to both, magnitude |u| |v| sin(θ).
Unit vectors: divide by magnitude. Direction cosines: cos(α), cos(β), cos(γ) with sum of squares = 1.
Applications: displacement, force, work, torque, positioning in 3D space.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vectors describe position, movement, force, and rotation in space—essential for physics and engineering.

subject: Mathematics
title: Akshay's Construction: Building in 3D Space
hook: An architect learns to work in three dimensions using coordinate geometry

slides.title: Three Dimensional Geometry
slides.storyContext: Akshay interns at an architecture firm in Mumbai. His first project: design a small pavilion. The architects use 3D coordinates to plan every beam, column, and roof angle. 'Geometry isn't flat,' Rukhsana tells him. 'It's three-dimensional, and math is the blueprint.'

slides.title: The Pavilion Blueprint
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana sketches a pavilion with four corners. She places the origin (0, 0, 0) at ground level, center. Corners are at A(2, 2, 0), B(−2, 2, 0), C(−2, −2, 0), D(2, −2, 0). Four columns rise at each corner to height 4 meters: A'(2, 2, 4), B'(−2, 2, 4), C'(−2, −2, 4), D'(2, −2, 4). A roof beam connects A' to C'. Akshay asks, 'How do I describe this in math?' Vikram (his friend who's good at geometry) says, 'With 3D coordinates, lines, planes, and distances.'

slides.title: 3D Coordinate System and Distance
slides.storyContext: Vikram teaches Akshay the 3D Cartesian system: three perpendicular axes (x, y, z) with origin O(0, 0, 0). Every point P is (x, y, z).

points.label: 3D Coordinates
points.text: Point P(x, y, z): x is distance along x-axis, y along y-axis, z (height) along z-axis.

points.label: Distance formula
points.text: Distance between P₁(x₁, y₁, z₁) and P₂(x₂, y₂, z₂) is d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²].

points.label: Section formula
points.text: Point dividing line segment P₁P₂ in ratio m:n is R = ((mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n), (my₂+ny₁)/(m+n), (mz₂+nz₁)/(m+n)).

example.solution: Roof beam is 4√2 ≈ 5.66 m long and its midpoint is at ground center, 4 m high.

slides.inSimpleWords: In 3D, use (x, y, z) to place points. Distance is found by extending the 2D formula to three dimensions.

slides.title: Direction Cosines and Ratios
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana points to a diagonal beam and asks Akshay, 'At what angles does this beam make with the x, y, z axes?' This is where direction cosines come in.

points.label: Direction cosines
points.text: For line from P₁(x₁, y₁, z₁) to P₂(x₂, y₂, z₂): direction numbers are (x₂−x₁, y₂−y₁, z₂−z₁). Direction cosines are (cos α, cos β, cos γ), where cos α = (x₂−x₁)/d, etc., and d is distance.

points.label: Identity
points.text: cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1.

points.label: Direction ratios
points.text: Often write as a:b:c (proportional to x-difference, y-difference, z-difference). Simplify by finding GCD.

example.problem: Diagonal column from A'(2, 2, 4) to opposite base corner C(−2, −2, 0). Direction numbers: (−2−2, −2−2, 0−4) = (−4, −4, −4) or simplified (−1, −1, −1) or (1, 1, 1). Distance = √(16 + 16 + 16) = √48 = 4√3. Direction cosines: cos α = −4/(4√3) = −1/√3, cos β = −1/√3, cos γ = −4/(4√3) = −1/√3. Verify: (−1/√3)² + (−1/√3)² + (−1/√3)² = 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1. ✓
example.solution: Direction ratios (1:1:1). Direction cosines (−1/√3, −1/√3, −1/√3), meaning the diagonal makes equal angles with all three axes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Direction cosines tell the angles a line makes with x, y, z axes. They always sum (as squares) to 1.

slides.title: Equation of a Line in 3D
slides.storyContext: Vikram shows Akshay how to write the equation of any line in space—essential for specifying beams and columns in the design.

points.label: Vector form
points.text: Line through point P₀(x₀, y₀, z₀) with direction ratios a:b:c is r = r₀ + t(a, b, c), where r₀ = (x₀, y₀, z₀) and t is parameter.

points.label: Parametric form
points.text: x = x₀ + at, y = y₀ + bt, z = z₀ + ct (t is parameter, can be any real number).

points.label: Symmetric form
points.text: (x − x₀)/a = (y − y₀)/b = (z − z₀)/c (requires a, b, c ≠ 0).

example.problem: Pavilion column from A(2, 2, 0) to A'(2, 2, 4). Direction: (0, 0, 4) or (0, 0, 1). Parametric: x = 2, y = 2, z = 0 + 1·t = t (for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4). Symmetric form: This is degenerate since x and y don't change. Better written as x = 2, y = 2, 0 ≤ z ≤ 4.
example.solution: Column equation: x = 2, y = 2, 0 ≤ z ≤ 4. It's a vertical line at (2, 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: A line in 3D needs a starting point and a direction. Parametric equations let you find any point on the line.

slides.title: Equation of a Plane
slides.storyContext: The roof of the pavilion is a flat plane. Rukhsana asks Akshay to describe its equation. This plane passes through four points at height z = 4.

points.label: General equation
points.text: Plane equation: ax + by + cz + d = 0, where (a, b, c) is normal vector to the plane.

points.label: Point-normal form
points.text: Plane through P₀(x₀, y₀, z₀) with normal (a, b, c): a(x − x₀) + b(y − y₀) + c(z − z₀) = 0.

points.label: Intercept form
points.text: Plane with x-intercept a, y-intercept b, z-intercept c: x/a + y/b + z/c = 1.

example.problem: Roof plane passes through A'(2, 2, 4), B'(−2, 2, 4), C'(−2, −2, 4), D'(2, −2, 4). All have z = 4. Normal vector points vertically: (0, 0, 1). Plane equation: 0(x − 0) + 0(y − 0) + 1(z − 4) = 0, so z = 4. Or general form: 0x + 0y + 1z − 4 = 0.
example.solution: Roof plane equation is z = 4. Any point on the roof has height exactly 4 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: A plane is defined by ax + by + cz + d = 0. The coefficients (a, b, c) are the normal direction perpendicular to the plane.

slides.title: Angle Between Lines and Planes
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana needs to know: (1) at what angle does a bracing diagonal meet a column? (2) at what angle does a slanted beam meet the roof plane?

points.label: Angle between two lines
points.text: Lines with direction ratios a₁:b₁:c₁ and a₂:b₂:c₂. cos θ = |a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂| / √(a₁² + b₁² + c₁²) √(a₂² + b₂² + c₂²).

points.label: Angle between line and plane
points.text: Line with direction (a, b, c); plane with normal (p, q, r). sin φ = |ap + bq + cr| / √(a² + b² + c²) √(p² + q² + r²).

points.label: Perpendicularity
points.text: Lines perpendicular if a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0. Line perpendicular to plane if (a, b, c) parallel to (p, q, r).

example.solution: The diagonal meets the column at about 54.7°. Structural engineers use this to calculate stresses.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles between lines and planes are found using dot products of direction and normal vectors.

slides.title: Full Problem: Roof Truss Design
slides.storyContext: Rukhsana designs a roof truss connecting two opposite roof corners A'(2, 2, 4) and C'(−2, −2, 4), with a central support at height 5 meters directly above the origin: S(0, 0, 5). Find (a) lengths of the two diagonal braces A'S and C'S, (b) equation of plane containing A', C', S, and (c) check if all three points are coplanar.

example.solution: Both diagonal braces are 3 meters long. The plane containing A', C', S is y = x. This defines the symmetry plane of the truss.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D geometry lets architects design complex structures by calculating distances, angles, and plane equations.

slides.title: Test Yourself: Corner Brace
slides.storyContext: A corner brace runs from A(2, 2, 0) to A'(2, 2, 4) and then to S(0, 0, 5). Find (a) total length of this path, (b) the straight-line distance from A to S.

points.text: (a) Length A to A' plus A' to S.
(b) Direct distance from A to S.

example.solution: Path length is 7 m; direct distance is √33 ≈ 5.74 m (shorter, as expected).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use distance formula repeatedly for paths with multiple segments.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) locate points in space.
Distance: d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²].
Lines: parametric (x=x₀+at, y=y₀+bt, z=z₀+ct) or symmetric ((x−x₀)/a = (y−y₀)/b = (z−z₀)/c).
Planes: ax + by + cz + d = 0. Normal vector (a, b, c) is perpendicular to plane.
Direction cosines satisfy cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1.
Angle between lines uses dot product of direction vectors.
Angle between line and plane uses dot product of line direction and plane normal.
Applications: building design, structural engineering, astronomy, navigation.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D geometry is the mathematical language of architecture and engineering. Coordinate systems, lines, and planes define space.

subject: Mathematics
title: Sophia's Bakery: Maximizing Profit
hook: A baker uses linear programming to decide what to bake for maximum profit

slides.title: Linear Programming
slides.storyContext: Sophia opens a small bakery in Delhi. Every day she has limited flour, butter, and oven time. Some days she bakes bread; other days, cakes. She wants maximum profit. Her brother Rahul says, 'This is a math problem'—it's linear programming.

slides.title: The Bakery Decision
slides.storyContext: Each day Sophia has: 10 kg flour, 2 kg butter. Bread uses 1 kg flour, 0.25 kg butter, takes 20 min, sells for ₹250 profit. Cake uses 1 kg flour, 0.5 kg butter, takes 30 min, sells for ₹400 profit. Oven capacity is 3 hours (180 min). How many breads and cakes should Sophia make to maximize profit? Rahul sketches constraints on a board. Ms. Chopra explains, 'This is linear programming—you have variables, constraints, and an objective to maximize.'

slides.title: What is Linear Programming?
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra starts the lesson. 'Linear programming solves real-world optimization problems where we have limited resources and want to maximize or minimize an outcome.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Linear Programming Problem (LPP): optimize (maximize or minimize) a linear objective function subject to linear constraints (inequalities or equalities) and non-negativity conditions.

points.label: Objective function
points.text: z = c₁x₁ + c₂x₂ + ... + cₙxₙ (profit, cost, etc. to optimize).

points.label: Constraints
points.text: Linear inequalities like a₁x₁ + a₂x₂ ≤ b (resource limits). Non-negativity: x₁, x₂, ... ≥ 0 (can't make negative items).

points.label: Feasible region
points.text: Set of all (x₁, x₂, ...) satisfying all constraints. Graphically, it's a polygon (in 2D) or polytope (in 3D+).

example.problem: Sophia's LPP: Let x = breads, y = cakes. Objective: maximize Z = 250x + 400y (profit). Constraints: (1) 1x + 1y ≤ 10 (flour), (2) 0.25x + 0.5y ≤ 2 (butter), (3) 20x + 30y ≤ 180 (oven time), (4) x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (non-negativity).
example.solution: This LPP describes Sophia's daily baking decision. The solution will be a point (x, y) where profit is highest while respecting all limits.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear programming finds the best combination of decisions when resources are limited and outcomes are proportional to decisions.

slides.title: Graphical Method (2D Problems)
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra draws the constraints on a graph. She shows Sophia how to find the feasible region—the polygon where all constraints are satisfied.

points.label: Step 1: Plot constraints
points.text: Draw each inequality as a boundary line. Shade the region where the inequality holds.

points.label: Step 2: Find feasible region
points.text: Intersection of all shaded regions is the feasible region (usually a convex polygon).

points.label: Step 3: Find corner points
points.text: Optimal solution lies at a corner (vertex) of the feasible polygon. Find all corner points.

points.label: Step 4: Evaluate objective
points.text: Calculate objective function Z at each corner. Maximum (or minimum) Z is the optimal value.

example.problem: Sophia's constraints: (1) x + y ≤ 10, (2) 0.25x + 0.5y ≤ 2, (3) 20x + 30y ≤ 180. Rewrite (2): x + 2y ≤ 8. Rewrite (3): 2x + 3y ≤ 18. Corner points of feasible region: O(0, 0), A(0, 4) [intersection of y-axis and x + 2y = 8], B(2, 3) [intersection of x + 2y = 8 and 2x + 3y = 18], C(6, 2) [intersection of x + y = 10 and 2x + 3y = 18], D(10, 0) [intersection of x + y = 10 and x-axis]. Check feasibility of each: O ✓, A ✓, B ✓, C ✓, D ✓. Evaluate Z = 250x + 400y at each: O: 0, A: 1600, B: 1700, C: 2300, D: 2500.
example.solution: Maximum profit is ₹2500 at D(10, 0): make 10 breads, 0 cakes. Sophia checks: 10 breads use 10 kg flour ✓, 2.5 kg butter. Wait, this violates butter constraint! Let me recalculate. Actually, x + 2y ≤ 8 means 10 + 0 ≤ 8? No, 10 > 8. So D is infeasible. Recheck: feasible corners are O(0, 0), A(0, 4), B(2, 3), C(4, 2). Evaluate Z: O: 0, A: 1600, B: 1700, C: 1800. Maximum is ₹1800 at C(4, 2): make 4 breads and 2 cakes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Draw constraints, find the feasible polygon, check corners, and pick the corner with highest (or lowest) objective value.

slides.title: Standard Form and Canonical Form
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra teaches Sophia how to convert any LPP into a standard form suitable for computer algorithms (like the simplex method).

points.label: Standard form
points.text: All constraints are ≤ inequalities (for maximization) or ≥ (for minimization). All variables ≥ 0. Objective is maximize or minimize. All constants on RHS ≥ 0.

points.label: Canonical form
points.text: Convert inequalities to equalities by adding slack variables (for ≤) or surplus variables (for ≥). Slack sᵢ ≥ 0; surplus eᵢ ≥ 0.

points.label: Slack variable example
points.text: Constraint x + y ≤ 10 becomes x + y + s = 10 (s ≥ 0 is unused resource).

points.label: Surplus variable example
points.text: Constraint 2x + y ≥ 8 becomes 2x + y − e = 8 (e ≥ 0 is excess).

example.problem: Sophia's LPP in canonical form: Maximize Z = 250x + 400y. Subject to: x + y + s₁ = 10, x + 2y + s₂ = 8, 2x + 3y + s₃ = 18, x, y, s₁, s₂, s₃ ≥ 0. Here, s₁ = unused flour capacity, s₂ = unused butter capacity, s₃ = unused oven time.
example.solution: In canonical form, the problem is ready for simplex method or matrix algorithms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Slack variables represent unused resources. Converting to canonical form makes the problem solvable by algorithms.

slides.title: Unbounded and Infeasible Solutions
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra warns Sophia, 'Not all LPPs have a solution. Sometimes the feasible region is empty (infeasible). Other times, profit can grow infinitely (unbounded).'

points.label: Feasible region
points.text: Must be non-empty for a solution to exist. If constraints contradict (e.g., x ≥ 10 and x ≤ 5), problem is infeasible.

points.label: Unbounded solution
points.text: If feasible region extends to infinity in direction of objective improvement, optimal value is unbounded (e.g., 'profit → ∞ as production → ∞').

points.label: Degenerate solution
points.text: If two or more constraints are tight (active) at optimal point, solution is degenerate.

example.problem: Example of infeasible: x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3, x + y ≤ 7. No point satisfies all three (5 + 3 = 8 > 7). Example of unbounded: maximize Z = 2x + 3y subject to x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (no upper limit). As x, y → ∞, Z → ∞.
example.solution: Sophia's bakery problem is neither unbounded nor infeasible because resources (flour, butter, time) are finite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always check if the feasible region exists and is bounded. Bad inputs lead to infeasible or unbounded problems.

slides.title: Sensitivity Analysis
slides.storyContext: Sophia asks, 'What if butter prices change? What if I can get more oven time? How does my answer change?' This is sensitivity analysis.

points.label: Shadow price (dual value)
points.text: Marginal value of one unit of a resource. If flour's shadow price is ₹50, producing 1 more bread (using 1 kg flour) increases profit by ₹50.

points.label: Range of feasibility
points.text: Range of RHS values (resource amount) over which optimal basis remains valid.

points.label: Range of optimality
points.text: Range of objective coefficients (prices) over which current solution remains optimal.

example.problem: Suppose Sophia's optimal is 4 breads, 2 cakes (profit ₹1800). Shadow price of flour = ₹100 means: if she gets 11 kg flour instead of 10, new profit ≈ ₹1900. Shadow price of butter = ₹300 means: if she gets 2.5 kg butter, profit ≈ ₹1950.
example.solution: Sensitivity analysis helps Sophia decide if buying extra butter (at a cost) is worth it. If butter costs ₹200/kg and shadow price is ₹300/kg, buy more!

slides.inSimpleWords: Shadow prices tell how profit changes when resource amounts change. Use them to decide if investing in more resources pays off.

slides.title: Full Solution: Sophia's Optimal Production
slides.storyContext: Ms. Chopra walks Sophia through the complete graphical solution. She finds all corner points of the feasible region and calculates profit at each.

example.problem: Feasible corners (verified): O(0, 0), A(0, 4), B(2, 3), C(4, 2). Profits: Z(O) = 0, Z(A) = 250·0 + 400·4 = 1600, Z(B) = 250·2 + 400·3 = 500 + 1200 = 1700, Z(C) = 250·4 + 400·2 = 1000 + 800 = 1800. Maximum is at C(4, 2) with profit ₹1800. Resource usage at C: flour = 4 + 2 = 6 kg (4 unused), butter = 1 + 1 = 2 kg (fully used), time = 80 + 60 = 140 min (40 unused).
example.solution: Sophia should bake 4 breads and 2 cakes daily to maximize profit at ₹1800. Butter is the binding constraint. If she wants more profit, she should invest in more butter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphical method finds the optimal corner by checking each vertex of the feasible region.

slides.title: Test Yourself: New Product
slides.storyContext: Sophia introduces pastries: 0.5 kg flour, 0.25 kg butter, 15 min oven, ₹300 profit. Formulate and solve the new LPP with x breads, y cakes, z pastries.

points.text: Objective: maximize Z = 250x + 400y + 300z.
Constraints: flour, butter, time, non-negativity.

example.problem: Constraints: 1x + 1y + 0.5z ≤ 10 (flour), 0.25x + 0.5y + 0.25z ≤ 2 (butter), 20x + 30y + 15z ≤ 180 (time), x,y,z ≥ 0. This is a 3-variable problem; graphical solution is hard (3D polytope). Use simplex method or software. Rough guess: maybe 5 breads, 0 cakes, 10 pastries? Check: flour = 5 + 0 + 5 = 10 ✓, butter = 1.25 + 0 + 2.5 = 3.75 > 2 ✗. Infeasible. Try 4 breads, 2 cakes, 0 pastries (our previous answer): profit = 1800. Try 0 breads, 0 cakes, 16 pastries? Flour = 8, butter = 4 > 2. Infeasible. Real optimum requires simplex/software.
example.solution: With 3 variables, graphical method isn't practical. Use simplex method or linear programming software (Excel Solver, Python PuLP, etc.).

slides.inSimpleWords: For 3+ variables, graphical method becomes impractical. Use algorithms (simplex) or software.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Linear Programming optimizes (maximize or minimize) a linear objective subject to linear constraints.
Feasible region: set of all solutions satisfying all constraints. Optimal solution lies at a corner.
Graphical method works for 2D. List all corners, evaluate objective at each, pick best.
Standard form: all ≤ constraints (or ≥), all variables ≥ 0, RHS ≥ 0.
Canonical form: convert ≤ to = by adding slack variables.
Shadow prices: marginal value of resources. Help decide if buying more resources is profitable.
Sensitivity analysis: how does solution change if parameters change?
Applications: production planning, diet problems, transportation, resource allocation, business strategy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear programming is the math of optimal resource allocation. Find the corner of the feasible region with the best objective value.

subject: Mathematics
title: Aditya's Cricket: Odds, Decisions, and Uncertainty
hook: A cricket analyst uses probability to predict match outcomes and make smart bets

slides.title: Probability
slides.storyContext: Aditya watches cricket matches and wonders: how likely is a win given the current score and weather? His friend Deepak (a sports journalist) says, 'That's probability. Let me ask Dr. Sharma to teach us.'

slides.title: The Cricket Match Prediction
slides.storyContext: India vs Pakistan in a Test match. After Day 1, India scores 300 in first innings, Pakistan replies. Dr. Sharma asks Aditya, 'What's the probability India wins?' Aditya says, 'I don't know—there are too many unknowns.' Dr. Sharma replies, 'Exactly. But we can assign probabilities based on historical data, current conditions, and Bayes' theorem. You can estimate it mathematically.'

slides.title: Sample Space, Events, and Basic Probability
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma starts with basics. 'Probability is about predicting uncertain outcomes. The sample space is all possible outcomes.'

points.label: Sample space (S)
points.text: Set of all possible outcomes. For one die roll: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

points.label: Event (E)
points.text: Subset of sample space. 'Rolling an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.

points.label: Probability
points.text: P(E) = (number of favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes). For fair die, P(even) = 3/6 = 0.5.

points.label: Axioms
points.text: (1) 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, (2) P(S) = 1, (3) P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F) if E, F are mutually exclusive.

example.problem: Coin toss: S = {H, T}. P(H) = 1/2. Two coins: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, all equally likely. P(at least one H) = 3/4.
example.solution: In cricket: if a bowler takes a wicket 20% of the time (on average), P(wicket next ball) ≈ 0.2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Probability is the chance of an outcome, ranging from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

slides.title: Conditional Probability and Independence
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma asks, 'Given it's raining, what's the probability of India winning?' This is conditional probability—probability of one event given another event has occurred.

points.label: Conditional probability
points.text: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), the probability of A given B has occurred.

points.label: Multiplication rule
points.text: P(A ∩ B) = P(A|B) · P(B) = P(B|A) · P(A).

points.label: Independence
points.text: Events A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A), i.e., B doesn't affect A. Then P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B).

points.label: Total probability
points.text: If B₁, B₂, ..., Bₙ partition S, then P(A) = Σ P(A|Bᵢ)·P(Bᵢ).

example.problem: Cricket: P(India wins | good batting form) = 0.7, P(good form) = 0.6. P(India wins) = 0.7 · 0.6 = 0.42. Also P(India wins | bad form) = 0.3, P(bad form) = 0.4, so P(India wins from bad form) = 0.3 · 0.4 = 0.12. Total: P(India wins) = 0.42 + 0.12 = 0.54.
example.solution: P(India wins) ≈ 0.54 or 54%, calculated using total probability over batting conditions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Conditional probability P(A|B) is the chance of A given we know B is true. Independent events don't affect each other.

slides.title: Bayes' Theorem
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma introduces Bayes' theorem. 'Suppose India wins. What's the probability they had good form?' This reverses conditional probability—going from effect to cause.

points.label: Bayes' theorem
points.text: P(B|A) = P(A|B) · P(B) / P(A). Reverses a conditional probability.

points.label: Terms
points.text: P(B) = prior (belief before data). P(A|B) = likelihood (data given belief). P(A) = evidence (observed data). P(B|A) = posterior (belief after data).

points.label: Application
points.text: Use Bayes to update beliefs as new information arrives.

example.problem: India won today. What's P(good form | win)? Using Bayes: P(good form | win) = P(win | good form) · P(good form) / P(win) = (0.7 · 0.6) / 0.54 = 0.42 / 0.54 ≈ 0.778 or 77.8%.
example.solution: After observing a win, Aditya updates his belief that India had good form to 78%. This is powerful for making decisions based on outcomes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bayes' theorem updates beliefs when new evidence arrives. Prior probability (old belief) × likelihood (new evidence) / evidence = posterior (new belief).

slides.title: Random Variables and Distributions
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma says, 'Let's define X = number of wickets India loses in one innings. X is a random variable—it can be 0, 1, 2, ..., 10 with different probabilities.'

points.label: Random variable
points.text: Function that assigns a numerical value to each outcome. Example: X = number of heads in 3 coin tosses; X ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}.

points.label: Probability distribution
points.text: For discrete X, P(X = x) for each possible value x. For continuous X, probability density function f(x).

points.label: Expected value (mean)
points.text: E(X) = Σ x · P(X = x) or E(X) = ∫ x · f(x) dx. Average outcome over many trials.

points.label: Variance
points.text: Var(X) = E[(X − E(X))²]. Measures spread. Standard deviation σ = √Var(X).

example.solution: On average, a die roll is 3.5. Most rolls deviate by about 1.71 from this mean.

slides.inSimpleWords: A random variable assigns numbers to outcomes. Its distribution shows probabilities. Mean is average; variance is spread.

slides.title: Binomial and Normal Distributions
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma explains the most common probability distributions used in real-world data.

points.label: Binomial distribution
points.text: X ~ B(n, p): n independent trials, each with success probability p. P(X = k) = C(n,k) · p^k · (1−p)^(n−k). Mean = np; variance = np(1−p).

points.label: Normal distribution
points.text: X ~ N(μ, σ²): continuous, bell-shaped, symmetric. Described by mean μ and std dev σ. PDF: f(x) = (1/(σ√(2π))) · exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)).

points.label: Central limit theorem
points.text: If X₁, X₂, ..., Xₙ are independent with same distribution, then sum (or average) approaches normal as n → ∞.

example.problem: Bowler takes 4 wickets per 20 balls (p = 0.2). In 100 balls, X = wickets taken. X ~ B(100, 0.2). E(X) = 100 · 0.2 = 20. Var(X) = 100 · 0.2 · 0.8 = 16. σ = 4. P(15 ≤ X ≤ 25) ≈ 0.68 (within 1 std dev of mean, by empirical rule of normal approximation).
example.solution: Bowler likely takes 15–25 wickets in 100 balls, with mean 20 and std dev 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Binomial counts successes in repeated trials. Normal is bell-shaped; most values cluster near the mean.

slides.title: Full Problem: Match Win Probability
slides.storyContext: India plays Australia in ODI. Historical data: India wins 50% of matches in Australia, 60% at home. Today's match is in Australia. India has a strong batting lineup today (good form), which increases win probability to 55% (vs 50% without). A rain forecast has 30% chance, which reduces win probability by 10 percentage points if it rains. Calculate P(India wins) using total probability.

example.problem: Define events: F = good form (P = 1), R = rain (P = 0.3). P(win | F, no R) = 0.55, P(win | F, R) = 0.45. No variation without form; assume it doesn't matter here. P(win) = P(win | no R) · P(no R) + P(win | R) · P(R) = 0.55 · 0.7 + 0.45 · 0.3 = 0.385 + 0.135 = 0.52.
example.solution: P(India wins) ≈ 0.52 or 52%. Good form and favorable conditions give slight edge, but rain risk lowers it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use total probability by conditioning on all relevant uncertainties (form, weather, venue, etc.).

slides.title: Test Yourself: Bayes and Sports
slides.storyContext: A player has a disease detection test. The test is 95% accurate (P(positive | diseased) = 0.95). Disease prevalence in population is 1% (P(diseased) = 0.01). Player tests positive. What's the probability they actually have disease?

points.text: Apply Bayes' theorem.
Calculate P(diseased | positive test).

example.problem: Let D = diseased, T+ = positive test. Given: P(T+ | D) = 0.95, P(D) = 0.01. Assume test is also 95% accurate at ruling out disease: P(T− | not D) = 0.95, so P(T+ | not D) = 0.05. P(D) = 0.01, P(not D) = 0.99. P(T+) = P(T+ | D)·P(D) + P(T+ | not D)·P(not D) = 0.95·0.01 + 0.05·0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059. P(D | T+) = P(T+ | D)·P(D) / P(T+) = (0.95·0.01) / 0.059 = 0.0095 / 0.059 ≈ 0.161 or 16.1%.
example.solution: Despite a positive test, probability of actually having disease is only ~16%, because disease is rare. This shows importance of considering prior probability!

slides.inSimpleWords: Even with a good test, a rare disease remains unlikely after a positive result. Bayes' theorem accounts for base rates.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Sample space S: all possible outcomes. Event E: subset of S. Probability P(E) = favorable / total.
Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B). Probability of A given B.
Independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B).
Total probability: P(A) = Σ P(A|Bᵢ)·P(Bᵢ) over partitions.
Bayes' theorem: P(B|A) = P(A|B)·P(B) / P(A). Updates beliefs with new evidence.
Random variable X: numerical outcome of experiment. Has distribution P(X=x) or f(x).
Expected value E(X): average outcome. Variance Var(X): measure of spread.
Binomial B(n,p): n trials, success probability p. Normal N(μ,σ²): bell curve.
Applications: sports predictions, medical testing, insurance, quality control, decision-making under uncertainty.

slides.inSimpleWords: Probability quantifies uncertainty and helps make decisions when outcomes are not certain. Use Bayes to update beliefs as evidence arrives.
